name: Tolvaptan

lead: Tolvaptan is a prescription drug that makes the body excrete free water, and it is occasionally raised in depuffing discussion for that reason.

It antagonizes the V2 vasopressin receptor in the kidney's collecting duct, reducing cAMP and water reabsorption, an effect called aquaresis that removes water without major electrolyte loss. It is approved for low blood sodium (Samsca) and for slowing kidney decline in polycystic kidney disease (Jynarque). No study has tested it for facial puffiness.

paras: It is a prescription tablet started under medical supervision, with monitoring in its approved uses. Increased urination follows within hours of a dose.

The Jynarque label has a boxed warning for serious, potentially fatal liver injury, with liver failure requiring transplant reported, and requires monthly liver tests early in treatment. It also warns of dehydration and abnormally high sodium, interacts with CYP3A inhibitors, and is prescription-only.

angle.text: Tolvaptan is a prescription drug that blocks vasopressin so the body excretes free water, and it is occasionally raised in depuffing discussion for that reason. Less retained water is the step people expect to lead to a less puffy face. It is approved for hyponatremia and kidney disease, with no appearance data.

lead: Tolvaptan is a prescription aquaretic: a selective vasopressin V2-receptor antagonist that makes the kidneys excrete free water without large losses of sodium and other electrolytes. In appearance terms, this water-shedding action is why it is listed under depuffing, the idea being that excreting retained water could leave the face, hands or midsection looking less swollen. Its approved purposes are medical: treating clinically significant hyponatremia (brand Samsca) and slowing kidney function decline in adults at risk of rapidly progressing autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, or ADPKD (brand Jynarque).[1][2][3]

Otsuka Pharmaceutical developed the drug. The US FDA approved Samsca on 19 May 2009 and Jynarque in April 2018, and a generic version has been available in the United States.[1][3] It is prescription-only in the US, UK, EU and Australia, and it appears on the World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list.[3]

No published study has tested tolvaptan for facial puffiness or cosmetic purposes. The Jynarque label carries a boxed warning for serious and potentially fatal liver injury, with acute liver failure requiring transplantation reported, and requires liver-test monitoring early in treatment.[2]
infobox: Oral (an IV prodrug, tolvaptan phosphate, also exists)[3]

paras: Hyponatremia: tolvaptan is approved for clinically significant euvolemic and hypervolemic hyponatremia, including cases from heart failure, cirrhosis and the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH). Grokipedia states treatment is started in hospital and limited in duration because of liver risk.[1] Reviews of hyponatremia management describe urea and tolvaptan as the most effective second-line options in SIADH when fluid restriction fails, while noting that evidence guiding the choice between second-line therapies is limited.[4][5]

ADPKD: the Jynarque label indicates it to slow kidney function decline in adults at risk of rapidly progressing disease.[2] ADPKD is the most common inherited kidney disorder, and a 2026 Lancet review describes the evidence base for tolvaptan as a disease-modifying treatment as strong, supporting its use in people at high risk of kidney failure.[6]

Tolvaptan binds the V2 receptor with an affinity the label puts at 1.8 times that of native vasopressin and 29 times its affinity for the V1a receptor. Blocking vasopressin lowers adenylate cyclase activity and cAMP in the kidney's collecting duct, which prevents aquaporin-2 vesicles from fusing with the cell membrane and so reduces water reabsorption.[2] The result, aquaresis, differs from loop-diuretic action because little sodium is lost with the water, a contrast the authors of the 2004 heart-failure trial drew with conventional diuretics.[7] Reviews of the vaptan class describe such non-peptide vasopressin antagonists.[8]

Wikipedia reports about 99 percent protein binding, hepatic metabolism mainly through CYP3A4, and a terminal elimination half-life of roughly 12 hours.[3] Because of CYP3A metabolism, the label warns about interactions with CYP3A inhibitors.[2]

The label's boxed warning concerns serious liver injury, and it directs liver-test monitoring before treatment, at 2 and 4 weeks, then monthly for the first 18 months and every 3 months afterwards.[2] It also warns of hypernatremia, dehydration and hypovolemia.[2] The most common adverse reactions in the ADPKD trials, each affecting more than 10 percent of participants and at least twice the placebo rate, were thirst, polyuria, nocturia, increased urinary frequency and polydipsia.[2]

In hyponatremia, overly rapid correction of sodium can cause osmotic demyelination syndrome, which can be fatal.[3] In a 2013 Drug Safety Communication, the FDA concluded that Samsca should not be used for more than 30 days or in patients with underlying liver disease.[3] Embryo-fetal studies in animals showed no developmental toxicity at maternally non-toxic doses, and human data are insufficient.[2]

Otsuka Pharmaceutical developed tolvaptan, whose development code OPC-41061 appears in registered trials.[1][9] Early placebo-controlled studies in heart failure appeared in 2003 and 2004, followed by the SALT hyponatremia trials in 2006 and the EVEREST programme in 2007.[10][7][11][12][13] The FDA approved Samsca in May 2009, and orphan-drug designation for ADPKD was granted in April 2012, and TEMPO 3:4 was published later that year.[14][3] The April 2018 approval of Jynarque made tolvaptan the first drug approved to address disease progression in ADPKD.[1][3]

Tolvaptan is a controlled prescription drug, and its use for fluid loss outside the approved conditions is not described in published research. The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibited list names it, reflecting that water-excreting drugs can be used to change body weight or to mask other substances.[3] The wiki found no community discussion documenting appearance-motivated use.
No studies found on tolvaptan for facial puffiness or cosmetic depuffing. Published trials cover hyponatremia, heart failure, cirrhosis and polycystic kidney disease.

Hyponatremia: two multicenter placebo-controlled trials (SALT) tested tolvaptan in euvolemic or hypervolemic hyponatremia with 448 patients, 223 assigned to placebo and 225 to tolvaptan, starting at 15 mg daily and titrated by serum sodium.[11] A later study reported oral tolvaptan to be effective in chronic hyponatremia.[15]

Heart failure: the 2004 JAMA trial in patients hospitalised with worsening heart failure and the EVEREST programme examined whether tolvaptan added to standard therapy increased net volume loss without worsening electrolytes or kidney function.[7][12][13] A 2020 trial of loop-diuretic resistance in acute heart failure also appears in the literature of fluid-removal strategies.[16] Cirrhosis: Phase 3 registrations tested tolvaptan tablets in cirrhotic ascites and hepatic edema.[17][18]

ADPKD: TEMPO 3:4 randomised 1,445 adults aged 18 to 50 to tolvaptan or placebo for three years; total kidney volume grew 2.8 percent per year on tolvaptan versus 5.5 percent on placebo, and liver enzyme elevations were more frequent with tolvaptan.[14][19] A later NEJM trial examined later-stage disease.[19] A paediatric randomised trial and a pharmacokinetic study in adolescents have also been reported.[20][21]
